one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with Liberal Party presidential bet Mar Roxas asking the Comelec to declare Manuel Antonio Roxas a nuisance candidate -- Mar's namesake being one of the 130 who filed COCs for the presidency, alongside 19 for VP and 172 for the 12 Senate seats. These high national posts require only five qualifications: natural-born citizenship, registered voter, ability to read and write, age (40 for President/VP, 35 for Senator), and residence (10 years for President/VP, 2 for Senator). The rationale for these simple qualifications is to give the least of our compatriots an even chance to become our country's leaders, per the constitutional principle that 'the State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service.' While the Constitution theoretically guarantees equal access, it accepts the reality -- per Pamatong v. Comelec (April 13, 2004) -- that 'the State has a compelling interest to ensure that its electoral exercises are rational, objective, and orderly,' since 'the greater the number of candidates, the greater the opportunities for logistical confusion ... a disorderly election is not merely a textbook example of inefficiency, but a rot that erodes faith in our democratic institutions.' Consequently the Comelec has been authorized by the Omnibus Election Code to cancel the COCs of nuisance candidates -- those who (1) put the election process in mockery or disrepute, (2) cause voter confusion by similarity of names, or (3) have no bona fide intention to run. Technically, nuisance candidates are not 'disqualified' because they may in fact possess all five qualifications; their COCs are merely cancelled on the three grounds. CJ agrees with Mar Roxas, but before COCs can be cancelled the Comelec must first ask alleged nuisance candidates to show their bona fides -- usually financial capacity and nationwide-campaign ability -- because 'due process is an indispensable part of our democracy.' The Comelec gave itself an early Dec 10 deadline to weed out nuisance candidates because it must print the automated ballots listing all qualified bets; only printed names can be voted upon and read by PCOS machines. The ballots are 'precinct-specific' -- Manila ballots cannot be used in Makati even where national candidates overlap. Turning to screening other job applicants, while the constitutionally prescribed qualifications for national elective offices are simple, those for appointive ones are difficult: SC Justices need only 2 of the 5 elective qualifications (natural-born, age 40) plus they 'must have been for 15 years or more a judge of a lower court or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines,' requiring a four-year preparatory law course, a four-year basic law course, and the bar exam (20% average pass rate). Justices must also be 'of proven competence, integrity, probity and independence,' and must pass the JBC -- which acts like the Comelec in screening judicial appointees, but with stricter processes including lengthy interviews, psychological tests, background checks, medical clearances. 88 applicants are vying for the six newly created Sandiganbayan slots, all undergoing JBC screening. In short, elective officials need no scholastic qualities, desirable character traits, or strict screening, while SC Justices must possess at least two academic degrees, pass the bar, and hurdle the JBC. He closes with the reform-by-rhetorical-question: elective officials should have some educational attainment like a college degree and character traits like integrity and honor before they are voted upon -- if appointive officials in lowly rungs are required to possess civil service eligibility including college degrees and moral character, why not the highest officials of our land?
